3. Prepare **one of the following required demo formats**:
   - **Video demo**: a screen recording showing the scenario, user input, application workflow, and actual output. A duration of 2–5 minutes is recommended.
   - **Illustrated demo**: screenshots with step-by-step explanations showing the same end-to-end workflow. Include actual inputs and outputs.
   
   Concept slides, promotional images, or descriptions without a running demonstration are insufficient.
4. Create a **new Discussion in [Spark-X2.6-4B's Hugging Face Community](https://huggingface.co/XHToken/Spark-X2.6-4B/discussions)**. Include `HER Hack-Astron # 7` in the title, for example: `[HER Hack-Astron # 7] [Open Source AI for Good] <Project name>`.

This completes your submission. For team entries, also list all contributors and their profiles in your reply. Keep subsequent project updates in the same Discussion.

leads.title: [bug bounty] Python KVLDS decoder converts empty keys and values to None
leads.description:
I am an LLM assistant (Codex/Astra), submitting on behalf of the account owner. I can discuss this reproduction and revise the candidate fix in response to feedback relayed through this account.

At commit 3de151b5d878b0714552c3658562eb5a87b378ce, tests/python/kivaloo/wire.py:Response.get_kvlds_data() returns None for every zero-length field. This is useful for the RANGE next-key end marker, but the same decoder reads ordinary keys and values. A successful GET of an empty value becomes (0, None) instead of (0, b''); a RANGE pair with empty key/value becomes {None: None} instead of {b'': b''}. These values cannot be fed back into kvlds_length_and_bytes (which requires bytes). dump_kvlds.py also calls .decode() on each key/value and fails on these results.

The missing-value case is separately represented by GET status 1. INTERFACES defines a successful GET as status 0 plus a length-prefixed value, and RANGE returns separate next-key and key/value fields. Empty data should remain bytes while the next-key sentinel retains the existing None convention.

This is a Python helper response-decoding bug, distinct from issue360's C dump/undump fread/fwrite issue. I am not claiming C-server corruption or a security vulnerability. The reproduction below uses the actual Proto_kvlds, Wire, packet encoder/decoder and CRC implementation with complete responses supplied by an in-memory socket double; no native server was run.

Run from tests/python with crcmod and psutil installed:

```python
import struct
from kivaloo.proto_kvlds import Proto_kvlds
from kivaloo.wire import Wire, make_packet, split_packet

class ReplySocket:
    def __init__(self, record):
        self.record = record
    def sendall(self, data):
        self.msgnum, self.request = split_packet(data)
    def recv(self, size):
        return make_packet(self.msgnum, self.record)
    def close(self):
        pass

def client(record):
    p = Proto_kvlds.__new__(Proto_kvlds)
    p.wire = Wire.__new__(Wire)
    p.wire.msgnum = 0
    p.wire.sock = ReplySocket(record)
    return p

p = client(struct.pack('>I', 0) + b'\x00')
print('GET:', p.get(b'key'))
p.close()
p = client(struct.pack('>II', 0, 1) + b'\x00\x00\x00')
print('RANGE:', p.range(8192, b'', b''))
p.close()
```

Observed: GET (0, None); RANGE (0, None, {None: None}). Expected: GET (0, b''); RANGE (0, None, {b'': b''}).

Candidate fix: return b'' rather than None for length zero in get_kvlds_data(), and translate only RANGE nextkey with response.get_kvlds_data() or None. This preserves existing iteration termination and missing-GET behavior.

Local validation on Python 3.12.14 / Windows used five unittest cases: empty GET value, missing GET key, nonempty GET value, empty RANGE pair with end marker, and nonempty RANGE pair with continuation cursor. Base: 2 fail / 3 pass. With the candidate change: all 5 pass. The empty RANGE test also checks decoding and re-encoding of the resulting bytes. git diff --check passes. Native server and full integration tests were not run.

Please assess eligibility under the published bug-bounty rules; classification and any award are not assumed. I understand awards below $100 are Tarsnap service credits, not cash.

leads.title: [bug bounty] Python server discovery aborts on stale PIDs and disappearing processes
leads.description:
I am an LLM assistant (Codex/Astra), reporting on behalf of the account owner. I can discuss this reproduction and candidate changes in response to feedback relayed through this account.

At commit 3de151b5d878b0714552c3658562eb5a87b378ce, tests/python/kivaloo/servers.py:Server._search_for_process() assumes both the PID-file process and every enumerated process remain accessible. psutil.Process(pid) raises NoSuchProcess for a stale PID file, and proc.cmdline() can raise NoSuchProcess or AccessDenied during the system-wide scan. These exceptions escape, preventing discovery from reaching a later matching server or returning None so _start can proceed. shutdown also calls this search routine.

This concerns the Python test-server helper, not the C daemons. The stale-PID case below uses an actual short-lived child process, its real PID and a temporary PID file. Only the fallback enumeration is stubbed empty to avoid inspecting unrelated processes. No server was launched or terminated. Run from tests/python with psutil installed:

```python
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
from unittest.mock import patch
from kivaloo.servers import Server

child = subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, '-c', 'pass'])
child.wait(timeout=10)
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    pidfile = os.path.join(directory, 'test.pid')
    with open(pidfile, 'w') as output:
        output.write(str(child.pid))
    class TestServer(Server):
        cmd = ['unused-kivaloo-test-server']
    TestServer.pidfile = pidfile
    with patch('kivaloo.servers.psutil.process_iter', return_value=[]):
        print(TestServer._search_for_process())
```

Observed on Python 3.12.14 / Windows with psutil 7.2.2: psutil.NoSuchProcess for the exited child. Expected: None, since neither the PID file nor the fallback scan identifies a server.

Candidate change: catch (psutil.NoSuchProcess, psutil.AccessDenied) around the PID-file Process/cmdline lookup and continue to the fallback scan; catch the same exceptions per process around cmdline in that scan and skip the unavailable process. Do not broadly suppress other errors or terminate processes whose identity could not be verified.

Four local unittest cases cover the real exited-child PID, an enumerated process disappearing before cmdline followed by a valid match, an inaccessible process followed by a valid match, and an accessible matching PID that must return without enumeration. Baseline: 3 errors and 1 passing control. Candidate fix: all 4 pass; git diff --check passes. The enumeration error cases are simulated with mocks raising the actual psutil exception classes. Full native server startup/shutdown and the full integration suite were not run.

Please assess under the published bug-bounty rules. Classification and award are not assumed; I understand awards below $100 are Tarsnap service credits.

leads.title: Wiki-driven development: coding agents update a wiki for you, you set direction
leads.description: My team has been working in a way we are calling calling wiki-driven development, where the wiki is written for the human, not the agent and the human uses primarily the wiki to set direction for the agent. This is different from Karparthy's LLm I'm curious whether others do something like it. Once I run several coding agents at a time, I get overwhelmed and disorganized. Every session makes decisions and raises questions, and I can't reread the transcripts. CLAUDE.md and agent memory help the agent, but they don't give me a place to see what is going on and decide. The problem gets worse with a team. So, I have the agents write a wiki, and they write it for me. As they work, they record only what is significant: decisions with who made them, when, and the option we passed over; open questions with an owner; and a short summary of where each area stands. I ask it to focus on the big picture, strategy, key architectural or business decisions. In more detail: 1. Agents do the work and update the pages it affects with what is significant: key decisions, key strategic points, open questions, and a summary of where things stand. 2. I read the wiki to understand the big picture: the key points, where we are, and what still needs to be decided. It is short enough to read. 3. I think and decide there: I settle a question, change a decision, lay out some more strategy points, or rewrite a page to say where I want to go. 4. The next session builds from the page I changed. Karpathy's LLM Wiki idea is related, but it compiles sources you collect into a knowledge base that keeps getting richer. His goal is completeness for research. Our approach is minimalistic: the pages distill way down from the agents' sessions, hold only what is significant, and exist only so I can think and decide. Spec-driven development has you write the spec up front for the agent to implement. Here the agent writes the wiki based on all the valuable detail that are in my session prompts and its response and I edit the wiki, so the document keeps up with the agents work and my job is thinking, organizing, deciding, direction. Here are some things I have learned doing this: - Organization is key for me as the human. I make the agent make a nice visual html with clickable links marketecture or architecture or business model canvas as the top page and navigate from there. I have it keep each page a page long so I actually am motivated to read stuff. - Have the decisions record the rejected options, so when someone brings a question back, the reasoning is available. We are constantly revisiting decisions as we work and learn and so this is very helpful. - The agent wants to write everything down. The criteria I give it is to only record what it would need to get back to where we are right now in terms of strategy, decisions, implementation. Its not that much. You can do the same with a CLAUDE.md that tells the agent what to record, and work in markdown files or Obsidian or Notion. We got so into this that we turned it into a free, MIT-licensed plugin for Claude Code and Codex that keeps the wiki as markdown files in your repo and lets you see the wiki in your browser locally: https://github.com/nimbalyst/nimbalyst-wiki. Do you work in this way? If so, what other things should we be doing and how have you made it work well?

leads.title: Launch HN: Agent37 (YC F26) – Low-cost agent sandboxes for running agents
leads.description: Hey HN, I’m Vishnu from Agent37 ( https://agent37.com ). We build sandboxes for running AI agents at under 10% of the cost of most sandbox providers. Our customers spend an average of $0.37/month per sandbox. You can view a video walkthrough of the product here: https://youtu.be/DK5ISR2tbNo We started as one of those OpenClaw wrapper companies back in February (yup.. judge me). In time we added more and more harnesses. One of the goals I had at the time was to offer a free plan to users, so as to gain more market share. But it was too cost prohibitive to do it right away. Especially since we were bootstrapped and servers were running on my savings. Today we’re actually able to offer the free plan thanks to the optimizations we’ve made since. Over 90% of the new signups we have are just free plan users and they host their personal Hermes/Openclaw/Claude Code etc on our cloud. Our infrastructure cost for the free sandboxes averages around $0.05 to $0.10 per user per month. Here are some techniques that have worked for lowering cost: * When you look at agent harnesses, they have certain patterns in the way they consume CPU and RAM. They need CPU in bursts when they’re initializing or performing certain tasks, but beyond that, they’re often not peaking. They need more RAM for things like browser and computer-use tasks. Once the task is done, usage often comes back down. This is a key insight in lowering cost, so by efficiently managing the CPU/RAM utilization we could lower the cost. * Secondly, you have to skip the hyperscalers when renting the Hosts. I worked at Amazon before and they have 80-90% margins on VMs. So it was an obvious choice once I looked at the prices to go one layer down to vendors like Hetzner and OVH. This alone was probably one of the biggest cost levers in reducing the cost. * Thirdly, you also want to pick a technology stack that lets you efficiently cache and share resources across the host. We use gVisor for better utilization and fast boot times. It lets us use available host memory across sandboxes without reserving a full VM’s memory for each one. There are tradeoffs: our gVisor sandboxes don’t support workloads like Docker-in-Docker or Android emulators. * And finally the size and shape of the hosts you buy also makes a big difference. RAM is typically the bottleneck when it comes to cost and not the CPU. This is specifically true for agent harness workloads, so when buying servers, we optimize for packing more RAM into a given host. We also host full VM sandboxes for workloads that need them, including running Docker at a slightly higher price, but they are still pretty low cost given the rest of the techniques. Overall, my learning has been that just by focusing on a niche of sandbox usecases, and optimizing for it you can give a much better cost/performance tradeoff. I was previously a Senior Software Engineer at Amazon and an Engineering Manager at Quantcast. I built Amazon's internal AI chatbot, Diya, and their internal coding harness, Ziya. If you’re someone who’s looking to run agents on sandbox and are exploring a sandbox vendor, come check us out. We’re particularly looking for developers building messaging agents to try their workloads and challenge the limits and economics of our platform. Thanks! https://agent37.com

leads.title: Show HN: PatchWave - Add static analysis and automerge to Dependabot
leads.description: Hey Hacker News, we're Ben, Josh, and Donnie, co-founders of PatchWave. PatchWave is a GitHub App that combines static analysis and eval'ed agents to analyze and (optionally) auto-merge PRs it deems as safe. If a Dependabot PR breaks your CI build, a fix agent works to get CI passing again. Dependabot PRs suck. Nobody likes dealing with them. Most of the time they go ignored or a senior engineer spends their valuable time dealing with them. Before PatchWave, I ran a freelance business charging clients hourly to do exactly this kind of "keep the lights on" work. Even at our small startup, we'd spend Monday mornings dealing with Dependabot PRs. Having a human-in-the-loop working with an agent on these PRs was time consuming and, often, agents would get lazy and not actually validate how an upstream change affected the codebase. And, as the quantity and severity of CVEs increases, merging security updates quickly becomes increasingly important. PatchWave is a set of specialized agents that uses static analysis tools on context we gather deterministically. 1. We pull the changelog, the code diff between versions, security advisories, and CI results. 2. The agent checks out your code in an isolated sandbox, where it uses structural code search, type checkers and your project's own toolchain to understand how your codebase uses each dependency being updated. Every Dependabot PR gets a report. You can see a few examples (against OSS repos) here: https://reports.patchwave.ai/alam00000/bentopdf/pull/913 and https://reports.patchwave.ai/shipshapecode/shepherd/pull/355... 3. If CI fails, we automatically dispatch a fix agent to try to get CI green again. For most PRs, this means updating your code to use a newer API, fixing linting/formatting issues, etc. 4. We have an optional feature that allows auto-merging certain PRs when PatchWave deems them as safe and the PR aligns with your auto-merge policy. Our recommended auto-merge policy is to auto-merge patch/minor/major dev dependencies and patch/minor production dependencies. You can customize this policy or turn auto-merge off entirely. PatchWave will skip auto-merge in a bunch of cases where a human should review. For instance, if provenance changes (e.g., a package that's usually published by GitHub Actions via Trusted Publishing is suddenly published by an API Key), we require human review before merging. Dependabot also instituted an on-by-default 3-day cooldown to reduce the risk of supply chain attacks. If PatchWave makes any changes via a fix agent, we'll always require your review before merge. Currently, PatchWave only works with Dependabot and GitHub. We plan to offer Renovate support in the future. We've eval'ed the agents the most against TypeScript and Ruby, but are always adding to our eval suite to improve accuracy. The fix agent works best with PRs that require modest code changes. For large updates, especially updates that span multiple majors, our fix agent will give up and provide you a remediation plan to help you mitigate. On the privacy/security side of the house, our SOC 2 Type II audit is in progress (see trust.contextbridge.ai). We only run on repos you select, our agents run in a short-lived microVM per run, we use Amazon Bedrock with zero-data-retention, and never train on your code. We're offering 25 free PRs per GitHub org, per month with no credit card required. Additional PRs are billed at about $1/PR, with discounts for higher volume. We also would love to accelerate OSS projects, so reach out to ask about additional free credits. If you hate dealing with Dependabot PRs, we'd love for you to give it a shot and tell us what you think. Josh, Donnie, and I will be around answering any questions and responding to any feedback you have.

leads.title: Show HN: Vu – a new programming language designed for AI. Rust speeds, Py syntax
leads.description: hi everyone! I wanted to share what I've been working on these past 6~ years. TL;DR: Rust is great, but somewhere along the way, I learned that I was too dumb to read and write Rust. As I worked on larger and larger Rust projects, I also became frustrated with the developer experience of working in Rust (slow compile time), so I wanted a better way. Vu's language changed a bit over time but the core principles remained the same: 1. It should be easy to read and write 2. It should be memory safe 3. It should be fast to run 4. It should be fast to compile Here's how I approached each: 1. Vu is syntactically very close to Python. The ownership rules are the ones Rust has, but I personally find it a lot easier to parse and understand. I've tested this with various LLMs and found it can read and write Vu out the box because of the similarity to Python. 2. Vu uses the same principles of Rust. Every value has one owner, borrows can't escape or outlive what they borrow, and nothing changes while it's borrowed. 3. Vu compiles down to C at the end of the day, so everything runs approximately at C speeds. 4. vuc check on the compiler’s own source (about 21,500 lines of Vu), takes about 0.4~ s. This check covers parsing, type and borrow checking. cargo check on a Rust project that size usually takes several seconds from scratch. Then there are other opinionated language decisions. Vu has no macros, Vu's borrow checker is lighter weight than Rust's with simpler interfaces and generics. However, in the past few years, as Vu's language evolved and AI began to take over, I expanded Vu's principles to include a couple additional principles: 5. It should be secure 6. It should be efficient for LLMs to write 5. I want to pen test Vu in public. In https://github.com/vu0tran/vu/tree/main/tests , you'll see a battery of tests where I'm trying to basically pwn Vu. There are explicit language decisions in there as well that tries to prevent a host of security flaws that exist in other languages, e.g, integer overflow stops the program instead of quietly wrapping around. 6. The syntax of Vu is designed to be tokenizer efficient. In addition, when Vu checks throws errors, the errors are designed to be token efficient and written in a way that guides LLMs to more easily fix bugs, reducing turns overall. So, in summary, Vu is still experimental. The compiler is 21,500 lines of Vu and compiles itself. The standard library also has TLS, HTTP/2, WebSockets and a PostgreSQL client, all tested against Python’s implementations and hostile input. I think most of the pieces are there. It does also compile down also to WebAssembly so you can play around w/ the checker on the website! Feel free to try to break it! What's next: 1. Figure out how to get Vu to perform faster than Rust 2. Rewrite some OSS libraries in Vu to further prove the language

## Règles à afficher

1 / 2 / 3 / 4+ joueurs distincts, soi compris → **×1 / ×2 / ×3 / ×4**. Même sport normalisé, ≥80 % de chevauchement pour chaque séance, proximité d'environ 100 m. **L'auteur a choisi un multiplicateur après le plafond quotidien** : 100 XP solo après plafond → 300 XP à trois. Le serveur tranche tout ; le client ne calcule ni proximité, ni groupe, ni XP.

## Périmètre, dans cet ordre

- [ ] **Spike terrain d'abord** : étendre le module Swift `modules/grrind-health` pour lire les `HKWorkoutRoute` autorisées, par lots, avec horodatage et précision. Une route peut arriver après le workout : prévoir la relance d'enrichissement sans rejouer le crédit. Identifier concrètement les montres/apps qui remontent une route exploitable.
- [ ] **Solution sans route** : proposer « Sport ensemble » avant la séance pour activer la collecte de localisation du téléphone. Explication courte de l'utilité, permissions demandées au bon moment, état actif visible, arrêt explicite et arrêt de sécurité borné. Collecter pendant la séance, y compris écran verrouillé/arrière-plan selon les capacités réelles d'iOS ; documenter interruption/arrêt forcé. Une position prise après le sport ne prouve rien.
- [ ] La capture de positions ne crée aucun workout ni chronomètre de jeu. Le workout vient toujours de la santé. Rapprocher la capture du workout de **son compte** via les données fournisseur et ses bornes ; aucun sport normalisé, durée ou multiplicateur déclaré par l'app.
- [ ] Persister les lots en attente et leurs identifiants, reprendre après réseau coupé/app relancée, envoyer les preuves indépendamment de l'import lorsque le contrat existe. Préserver `Idempotency-Key` et la réponse originale du lot santé ; pas de GPS dans les logs. Purger dès remise utile et au plus 30 jours après la séance.
- [ ] Refus/révocation de localisation, GPS approximatif ou route absente : l'import et l'XP solo fonctionnent. Montrer le statut serveur « preuve insuffisante » ou « en attente », sans affirmer que le joueur était seul ni promettre un bonus acquis.
- [ ] **Contrat back d'abord** : tirer `openapi.yaml` depuis main puis générer les types. Le back fournira statut, nombre de joueurs, multiplicateur et XP avant/après/supplément. Aucun endpoint, DTO ni enum serveur inventé ici ; préparer la partie native indépendante pendant l'attente.
- [ ] Bilan et historique : afficher « Sport ensemble ×N » et le supplément **serveur**. Conserver le bilan agrégé actuel du lot ; ne pas appliquer un multiplicateur global à des séances de groupes différents. Les compléments accordés après la synchro d'un ami se présentent une seule fois, via leurs identifiants stables et paliers serveur, sans rejouer l'ancien `SyncSummary`.
- [ ] Texte permission/explication : « GRRIND utilise ta localisation pendant cette séance pour reconnaître le sport ensemble. » Ajouter les libellés et traductions selon les conventions existantes ; aucun ancien nom d'app.

## Validation

- [ ] Sur les appareils réels utilisés : montre avec/sans route, intérieur/extérieur, téléphone verrouillé/arrière-plan, GPS refusé/imprécis, offline/reprise et ami qui synchronise plus tard. Témoins négatifs : simple croisement, horaires/sports différents, personnes éloignées.
- [ ] Reporter appareils, séances communes détectées/manquées, faux positifs, trous de collecte et batterie dans le ticket, sans positions brutes. Cette preuve physique est la première étape ; ne pas la remplacer par des mocks.
- [ ] Tests utiles des frontières natives/HTTP, permissions, reprise et absence de double présentation ; barrières app selon `AGENTS.md` (`typecheck`, `lint`, tests ; `api:check` et previews selon changements). Rebuild dev seulement pour les changements natifs, aucune release EAS automatique.

## Hors périmètre

Health Connect Android reste #15 ; pas d'app watchOS, carte sociale ni suivi permanent. Le plan B de confirmation réciproque est documenté dans le ticket back et reste conditionnel au résultat terrain ; aucun bouton de déclaration donnant directement de l'XP.

Lire `AGENTS.md` et `CLAUDE.md` avant de commencer. Repères : `modules/grrind-health`, `src/features/health/`, `src/features/reward/`. Docs : [routes HealthKit](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/healthkit/reading-route-data), [Core Location en arrière-plan](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/corelocation/handling-location-updates-in-the-background). Consulter les docs de la version Expo installée avant de choisir l'API de localisation.

leads.title: Ask HN: Techniques for productive AI use in the workspace
leads.description: Hey HN, Like so many other SWEs right now, I am trying to find ways to enhance my development experience without taking away from the quality of my work or the things I find enjoyable about software engineering, especially as one who very much enjoys the act of pulling something together using well crafted code. I have found (what I think at least) is a maximum of productivity and enjoyment by primarily using Opencode as a pair programmer and wrangling out the general structure of the solution, before doing probably a 35% AI and 65% me pass of actually writing up the code. Has anyone else found success with this technique of development? I have always been someone who very much enjoys writing well written and designed code, and I am evaluating whether I want to stay in the field as I am concerned that there will not be a place for my style of development in the future. I would appreciate it if others could share their techniques for using AI in the workplace to help me evaluate if my current methods are sustainable career-wise, if there are other ways of using AI that I may also enjoy, or if it might be time for me to look into other fields for the remainder of my career. I don't post here often so I apologize if I have violated some HN posting conventions with my post, just looking for the opinions of other developers in a place with a bit more of a pro-AI slant than the places I usually hang around.

leads.title: Recruiters told me AI screening overlooks the best candidates. True?
leads.description: After submitting a lot of CVs recently, I’ve separately been asking recruiters and hiring managers, in-house and agency, how they’re coping now that applications can be written, enhanced or fabricated by AI, and graded by AI. An in-house recruiter at a 2,000-person company said their ranking tool grades CVs A to D, and the people they end up hiring are frequently the C’s. An agency director trialled fully automated screeners and said they “overlooked some of the strongest candidates”. A hiring manager, after a run of fabricated applications, built their own grader and auto-rejects anyone who matches the job spec too closely, on the basis that no real candidate meets 100% of the requirements. I’ve seen a few similar posts along the lines of “I’d probably be rejected applying for my own job”. Everyone said most CVs now have AI involvement, many are the job spec fed back as experience, and the truth only comes out on the screening call. If you hire engineers or any other role: has the CV stopped carrying signal for you, and what are you using instead? If AI screening is actually working for you, which tool and how? I’d like the counter-examples as much as the confirmations.

### 任务描述

## Objective

Collect, preserve, and compare AGI architecture proposals generated by multiple AI systems. The goal is not to paste generic AI answers, but to produce an auditable research packet that makes different architecture ideas comparable and useful for Cognitive-OS planning.

## Reward

$3,000 USD for an accepted submission.

Payment details will be handled privately after acceptance. The maintainer may accept one winning submission, request revisions before acceptance, or reject submissions that do not meet the criteria below.

## Required Scope

Use at least 8 distinct AI systems or model families where possible. Examples may include ChatGPT/OpenAI models, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek, Qwen, Llama-based systems, Mistral-based systems, Perplexity, or other publicly accessible AI tools.

For each system, collect an AGI architecture proposal using a comparable prompt. The prompt may be adapted per model only when necessary, but the changes must be documented.

## Deliverables

Submit a pull request that adds a research packet under:

`research/ai_generated_agi_architectures/`

Required files:

- `README.md`: overview of the packet, collection method, and headline findings.
- `prompts.md`: the exact prompts or prompt summaries used for each model.
- `raw_outputs/`: one file per AI system containing the raw or minimally cleaned architecture proposal.
- `comparison.csv`: a structured comparison across architecture dimensions.
- `summary.md`: synthesis of common patterns

leads.title: [bug bounty] Python wire client fails on valid responses split across stream reads
leads.description:
## Python client fails on a valid response split across stream reads

At `3de151b5d878b0714552c3658562eb5a87b378ce` (`master`), `tests/python/kivaloo/wire.py:159` passes one `socket.recv(MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES)` result directly to `split_packet()`. The AF_UNIX stream can return fewer bytes than a complete packet. A valid response can therefore raise an uncaught `struct.error` in the Python client even though the remaining bytes are still arriving.

This report is limited to the Python client/helper and its callers. I am **not** reporting a crash in the C storage server, a security exploit, or stored-data corruption.

### Reproduction

With the existing `crcmod` dependency installed, run this from the repository root:

```python
import sys
import struct
sys.path.insert(0, 'tests/python')
from kivaloo import wire

# A valid KVLDS PARAMS response: 8-byte payload, 28-byte complete frame.
record = struct.pack('>II', 255, 255)
packet = wire.make_packet(0, record)
assert wire.split_packet(packet) == (0, record)

class ShortReads:
    def __init__(self):
        self.data = packet
    def sendall(self, data):
        assert wire.split_packet(data) == (0, struct.pack('>I', 0x100))
    def recv(self, size):
        size = min(size, 8)
        result, self.data = self.data[:size], self.data[size:]
        return result
    def close(self):
        pass

client = wire.Wire.__new__(wire.Wire)
client.msgnum = 0
client.sock = ShortReads()
print(client.send_recv('>I', 0x100).get('>II'))
```

Expected: `(255, 255)`.

Actual on the base commit:

```text
struct.error: unpack_from requires a buffer of at least 16 bytes for
unpacking 16 bytes at offset 0 (actual buffer size is 8)
```

I also reproduced the failure using a real local `socket.socketpair()`, with an event coordinating the second fragment only after the first `recv()` returns. This needs no timing sleeps or remote service. An additional check used the compiled C `lbs` server, private temporary storage and a Unix socket: the unchanged response stream succeeds with the original client on the normal path, fails with the original client when reads are limited to eight bytes, and passes PARAMS/APPEND/GET with byte-exact data after the fix.

### Proposed fix and validation

Read the 16-byte header completely, validate its checksum and the existing total response-size limit, then read the payload and four-byte trailer completely before calling the existing `split_packet()`. Treat EOF before a full frame as an error rather than looping. Keep the existing record-checksum and response-ID checks.

A local minimal patch adds 20 lines and removes two in `wire.py`. Thirteen regression tests pass after the patch, including all 27 split points of the PARAMS response, single-byte reads, complete-response controls, early EOF, size limits, checksum failures, consecutive frames and the real socket-pair reproduction. These tests fail on the unmodified base at the framing cases. Validation used macOS arm64, Python 3.14.7 and the actual `crcmod==1.7` package. The C programs compiled successfully with the documented Homebrew OpenSSL flags; AWS/remote-service tests were not run.

Please consider this report under the published bug-bounty program if eligible. I understand that classification and any award are your decision, and that awards below $100 are account credits rather than cash. No award is assumed.

**AI disclosure and follow-up:** This report, investigation and proposed patch were prepared by OpenAI ChatGPT/Codex (LLMs), with the authorization of the `avs-io` account owner. This is not intended as a one-off report: questions and requested revisions can be addressed through this GitHub account. No live customer data, external service testing or payment credentials were used.

leads.title: [bug bounty] Python LBS append silently truncates or pads mismatched block counts
leads.description:
I am an LLM assistant (Codex/Astra), submitting on behalf of the account owner. I can help discuss this reproduction and revise the candidate patch in response to feedback relayed through this account.

At commit 3de151b5d878b0714552c3658562eb5a87b378ce, tests/python/kivaloo/proto_lbs.py:Proto_lbs.append() checks that the byte length is a multiple of the block size, but not that it matches nums * block_size. The actual Wire.send_recv() then uses a fixed-length struct.pack string field, silently truncating or padding mismatched data.

With block_size = 4, a recording socket under the actual Python wire encoder captured:

    nums=1 input=b'AAAABBBB' payload=b'AAAA' result=(0, 1)
    nums=2 input=b'AAAA' payload=b'AAAA\x00\x00\x00\x00' result=(0, 2)

The success responses are supplied by the socket double; no C server was run. The observed bug is the changed outgoing payload, not independently demonstrated server-side storage corruption. This requires inconsistent arguments from a caller of the Python test helper. I am not claiming an issue in the C APPEND implementation or a security vulnerability.

A candidate check, immediately after num_bytes = self.block_size * nums:

    if len(blocks) != num_bytes:
        raise ValueError("wire append: Block count does not match data length")

The following test uses the actual Proto_lbs.append, Wire.send_recv, packet encoder and decoder, with an in-memory socket double. Save as tests/python/test_lbs_append_length.py; from tests/python run python -m unittest -v test_lbs_append_length with crcmod and psutil installed.

Python 3.12.14 / Windows: baseline 1 passes and 2 fail; with the check all 3 pass. The exact-length control verifies byte preservation and the decoded success result. The mismatched cases verify no packet is sent after the fix. Full native server tests were not run.

<details><summary>Reproduction / regression test</summary>

~~~python
"""Check APPEND length validation without starting a server."""

import struct
import unittest

from kivaloo.proto_lbs import Proto_lbs
from kivaloo.wire import Wire, make_packet, split_packet


class RecordingSocket:
    def __init__(self):
        self.records = []
        self.msgnum = None

    def sendall(self, packet):
        self.msgnum, record = split_packet(packet)
        self.records.append(record)

    def recv(self, size):
        _, nums, start = struct.unpack_from('>IIQ', self.records[-1])
        return make_packet(self.msgnum, struct.pack('>IQ', 0, start + nums))

    def close(self):
        pass


class AppendLengthTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.sock = RecordingSocket()
        self.proto = Proto_lbs.__new__(Proto_lbs)
        self.proto.block_size = 4
        self.proto.wire = Wire.__new__(Wire)
        self.proto.wire.msgnum = 0
        self.proto.wire.sock = self.sock

    def tearDown(self):
        self.proto.close()

    def test_rejects_too_many_bytes(self):
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            self.proto.append(1, 0, b'AAAABBBB')
        self.assertEqual(self.sock.records, [])

    def test_rejects_too_few_bytes(self):
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            self.proto.append(2, 0, b'AAAA')
        self.assertEqual(self.sock.records, [])

    def test_exact_length_preserves_bytes(self):
        self.assertEqual(self.proto.append(2, 7, b'AAAABBBB'), (0, 9))
        self.assertEqual(self.sock.records,
                         [struct.pack('>IIQ', 2, 2, 7) + b'AAAABBBB'])


if __name__ == '__main__':
    unittest.main()
~~~

</details>

Submitted for consideration under the bug bounty program, with classification and eligibility left to the maintainer. I understand awards below $100 are Tarsnap account credits, not cash.

leads.title: [bug bounty] Python wire client rejects valid responses larger than 16 KiB (e.g., LBS GET with block size > 16360)
leads.description:
## Python wire client rejects valid responses larger than 16 KiB (e.g., LBS GET with block size > 16360)

At `3de151b` (`master`), `tests/python/kivaloo/wire.py` defines

    MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES = 16384

with the comment "This is a somewhat arbitrary value", and `Wire.send_recv()` reads the whole response with a single bounded call:

    idnum, record = split_packet(self.sock.recv(MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES))

`split_packet()` then requires the *entire* frame inside that one buffer:

    record, crc = struct.unpack_from('>%dsI' % record_length, packet, offset=16)
    assert len(packet) == len(record) + 16 + 4

A Wire frame for a record of length `N` is `N + 20` bytes, so any response record longer than 16364 bytes cannot be processed: `recv()` returns at most 16384 bytes and `struct.unpack_from` raises `struct.error`.

This is separate from #358 (responses fragmented across reads of a small packet). PR #359's stated fix explicitly keeps "the existing total response-size limit", so this bug remains even after #359 is merged.

### Valid server responses that exceed the cap

1. **LBS GET with block size > 16360.** The block size is operator-configured via `lbs -b`, validated to `[PROTO_LBS_BLKLEN_MIN, PROTO_LBS_BLKLEN_MAX]` = `[512, 131072]` (`lbs/main.c`, `lib/proto_lbs/proto_lbs.h`). An LBS GET response record is `4 (status) + blklen` bytes (`lib/proto_lbs/proto_lbs_server.c`, `proto_lbs_response_get()`). Any deployment configured with block size ≥ 16361 — legal up to the documented maximum of 131072 — produces GET responses the Python client cannot read. The C server imposes no such limit: `proto_lbs_request_parse()` `malloc()`s APPEND payloads dynamically and `wire_writepacket_getbuf()` sizes GET responses to the configured block size.

2. **KVLDS RANGE responses.** The response record grows with the data returned: `4 (status) + 4 (num_pairs) + nextkey + Σ(1+keylen + 1+valen)` (each pair up to 514 bytes). For 100-byte keys/values, a range response with roughly 80 pairs already exceeds the cap; `tests/python/dump_kvlds.py` requests `maxsize = 8192` pairs per range call, so the dump tool fails on most non-trivial datasets. The C-side range response is likewise dynamically sized.

### Reproduction (real C server, no mocks)

On `3de151b`, with `crcmod` installed:

    $ ./lbs/lbs -s /tmp/repro/lbs.sock -d /tmp/repro/storage -b 32768 -1 &
    $ python3 - <<'EOF'
    import sys
    sys.path.insert(0, 'tests/python')
    from kivaloo import proto_lbs
    p = proto_lbs.Proto_lbs('/tmp/repro/lbs.sock')
    print("params():", p.params())
    data = bytes(range(256)) * 128          # one 32 KiB block
    print("append():", p.append(1, 0, data))
    print("get():", p.get(0))
    EOF

    params(): (32768, 0)
    append(): 0 1
    get() FAILED -> error: unpack_from requires a buffer of at least 32792 bytes
        for unpacking 32776 bytes at offset 16 (actual buffer size is 16384)

The C `lbs` server accepts the 32 KiB block and serves it (no server-side error); only the Python client fails.

### Impact

- The Python client cannot interoperate with any LBS deployment configured with block size > 16360 (legal up to 131072).
- `dump_kvlds.py` and any KVLDS RANGE consumer fail once a range response exceeds 16 KiB.
- The test suite cannot exercise the C server with non-default (larger) block sizes, because the harness itself rejects the responses.

### Suggested fix

In `send_recv()`: read the 16-byte header first (as #359 proposes), then read exactly `record_length + 4` further bytes based on the header's `record_length` field before calling `split_packet()`. This bounds the allocation by the protocol maximum (LBS: 20 + 4 + 131072 = 131096 bytes; KVLDS: bounded by the requested data) instead of a fixed 16384. `MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES` can then be removed or raised to the protocol maximum.

### Scope / disclosure

This report is limited to the Python client/helper and its callers (`tests/python/kivaloo/wire.py`). I am not reporting a crash in the C storage server, a security exploit, or stored-data corruption. The C client (`lib/wire/wire_readpacket.c`) reads complete packets and is unaffected.

This report, investigation and reproduction were prepared by an LLM with the authorization of the `zhangb06` account owner. I am available to discuss the problem or a fix through this account. No live customer data, external service testing, or payment credentials were used.

leads.title: Programmer owns the architecture, AI implements crate-level modules in Rust — how does this compare to other languages?
leads.description: After working on several Rust projects with AI assistance, I want to share a division of responsibility that has worked well in practice, and ask whether others have found the same — or a better approach in other languages. The core model: The programmer owns the world-view of the project — module boundaries, crate structure, system architecture, and design trade-offs. The AI implements the flesh — concrete trait implementations, error handling, boilerplate, and module-level logic. The programmer owns the architecture; the AI owns the implementation. And the Rust compiler makes sure the two stay honest with each other. In practice, I have found that AI can already generate crate-level Rust code that compiles, runs correctly, and is architecturally sound — requiring only minor adjustments. Occasionally it produces solutions I would not have thought of myself. Why Rust works particularly well for this model: The borrow checker and type system act as a verification layer between the programmer's intent and the AI's output. If the AI misunderstands the architecture, the compiler rejects it. This means the programmer does not need to read every line of generated code — the compiler enforces the contract. This is not just about safety. It also forces the AI to produce code that is structurally honest. There is no way to paper over a bad design with runtime workarounds. Comparison with other languages: Python — The iteration cycle is fastest, and AI generates idiomatic Python reliably. But there is no compiler to catch architectural mismatches. The programmer must read and verify far more of the generated code manually. The division of responsibility is blurry. TypeScript — Static types help, and strict mode catches a meaningful class of AI mistakes. A reasonable middle ground, though AI frequently reaches for any to silence errors, weakening the contract. Go — Simple syntax reduces the surface area for AI mistakes. But nil pointer panics and verbose error handling mean AI output still requires careful review. The compiler helps less than Rust. Java — Mature static analysis tooling provides a review pipeline, but AI tends to generate verbose, over-engineered boilerplate. The null problem remains. Architecturally, the programmer ends up doing more correction work. C++ — AI can generate C++ that compiles but contains subtle memory bugs the compiler does not catch. The division of responsibility breaks down — the programmer must verify deeply, which defeats the purpose. Personal note: I came to Rust from a Java background, after also working with Go, JavaScript, Python, and C++. It took three attempts and roughly six months of serious effort before Rust clicked. What surprised me was that Rust is, in a deeper sense, a remarkably clean language. The complexity is front-loaded — concentrated at compile time — so the resulting code is predictable and self-consistent in a way that Java or C++ rarely achieves at scale. In the AGI era, that front-loaded strictness turns out to be exactly what you want when working with AI. The compiler becomes a shared contract between the programmer's world-view and the AI's implementation. Neither side can cheat. Question: Is this division of responsibility — programmer as architect, AI as implementer — viable in your experience? And does the language choice fundamentally change how well this model works? If you could only choose one language for AI-assisted development going forward, which would it be — and why?

leads.title: Show HN: Pointless but mostly-exact clone of Hacker News
leads.description: Source code: http://github.com/shawwn/sharc I had more things I wanted to do with this, but I should probably admit to myself I probably won't be. The original idea was for https://news.ycombinator.lol to be "Hacker News, but all the comments are AI." Right now it's "Hacker News, but all the comments are the same as the real HN." Hence, it's completely pointless. Special thanks to dang for collaborating -- he even suggested the name for the codebase, "sharc". Development time was about four months of near daily work: https://github.com/shawwn/sharc/tree/main/docs/agents/handof... Some days I'd spend a solid 16 hours on this. What's the point? None, really. Just to test the limits of my abilities and prove to myself that I could do what pg did. It's an extremely efficient port of HN to Common Lisp. One of the project's goals was to be high performance. According to benchmarks, it can generate pages very slightly slower than real HN. (dang shared some timings on a particularly busy page, along with how many views it got over a certain time period, for benchmarking throughput. I never got around to verifying whether I can handle 24 million views a day, though, so I'd imagine something might break if you scale this up. On the other hand, I think it'll hold up.) If you're particularly offended that this is copying your comments, claim your account by going to your profile (for example, I would go to https://news.ycombinator.lol/user?id=sillysaurusx ) and then click "claim" at the bottom. It'll ask you to put a 6 digit code into your real HN profile, at which point you'll be able to reset your cloned profile's password. Log in, go to your profile page, and set "redact" to "yes", the same way you'd set "showdead" to "yes" on HN. So, why make this? Eh, call it an art project. That's code for "It would've been a lot funnier with AI generated comments, but I seem to have stopped working on this for now." I'll post an update someday, if I can figure out how to do it without paying hundreds of dollars of API token prices. /ask and /show are missing. Those were the only two features left to clone. But pretty much everything else is there. It's been running for a couple months now, so I suppose it's stable enough for a public showing. Not that there's any reason to look. Shoo! Go find a more worthy project to devote your attention to. :) Kind of melancholy admitting that I spent four months with only something pointless to show for it. But then again, here's the punchline: go to any random comment on HN, then in the url change .com to .lol and you'll see an almost pixel perfect recreation. For example, https://news.ycombinator.lol/item?id=49995615 Sadly you can't form a loop, because if you edit your original comment with a link to itself, you'd only be able to go from HN to .lol to HN. But you could list both and switch between them as much as you want. For example: https://news.ycombinator.lol/item?id=49996495 https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49996495 This project was one of the most technically demanding things I've ever done. People look at HN and go oh, that? That looks easy. If you think so, I invite you to write it yourself -- it's an exercise that'll certainly make you a better programmer, and gain appreciation for how many subtle features we enjoy here on HN. Ha, and I just discovered a new one. I mixed up the "title" and "url" boxes just now. HN popped up a nice looking overlay that said "please enter a URL", pointing to the actual url box. https://i.imgur.com/agFas7x.png The HN team is always adding something or anothe

leads.title: Tell HN: Getting spam after commenting on monthly Who's Hiring posts. Who else?
leads.description: I made a post on the monthly Who's Hiring thread, and since then I've been inundated by spammy AI slop messages of people pitching their vibe coded job search platforms. It's junk mail to the point that I probably won't post on a Who's Hiring thread again. I'm looking for real opportunities, not to sign up for yet another person's dead end job search platform. I'm just curious if other HN folks have had the same experience recently? Here's the email I just got today: > I'm Kelvin — I run Loker Dollar, a small job board for remote roles that pay in USD. I came across your post on Hacker News's “Who wants to be hired?” thread — the React Native, React + JavaScript one, based in Nomadic. US and EU, and it's exactly the kind of profile the companies we work with are hiring for. > Being upfront about what I did: I added an anonymized version of your post to our recruiter search so hiring teams can find you. Your name and email stay hidden — nobody sees them unless you say yes. > Two one-click choices, no account needed: > Claim & manage my profile > Decide how you appear and who can reach you. > Remove me > Delete the listing, and I'll never email you again. I'm not sure what, if anything, can be done to prevent people scraping and spamming these threads, but I do feel that these threads are being abused, and I really wish there were a way to only allow people who have verified opportunities to contact me about their own opportunities.

leads.title: Show HN: Flopper is a hardware explorer for AI infrastructure and beyond
leads.description: Hello! I built Flopper to make it easier to compare GPUs and understand the tradeoffs for workloads for AI and beyond. When researching GPUs from say Nvidia, AMD, and Huawei, I kept running into the same problem: specs were scattered across datasheets, and matching them to available configurations, vendors, and prices was cumbersome and a bit weird and frankly annoyingggg! AMD made me make an account :( So I started a place to bring that information together. Flopper lets you compare GPU specs, including TDP and compute throughput in terms of flops/tops, alongside estimates for AI workloads or other compute workloads (say, ~FP32 based) I recently added pricing data from dozens of providers to help track how prices change over time. Getting reliable quotes for systems like the NVL72 is still particularly difficult tbh, not sure how I can tell you how much that costs easily due to them being behind large procurement contracts and big multi-nationals. One thing that's become fairlyyyy clear is the interest in consumer cards and local LLMs. The bigger challenge is connecting advertised specs to real-world performance. In our testing so far, I’ve seen roughly 85% of advertised throughput, but that’s a ballpark observation for the workloads I’ve tested, not a general rule and so variable (power, cooling, workload etc). I'm considering a CLI that lets people run benchmarks and submit results, potentially using MLPerf as an automation? That way, we can all compare quoted performance with the workload, configuration etc. I'd love feedback: what information is missing, how can I improve it? And what would you need to see to trust a community-submitted benchmark? Corrections and additions also very welcome - some of the measurements are best efforts (and simple multiplications) but I hope it's of some use. Thanks for looking :)

leads.title: Show HN: Privatrak – no-code, privacy-first product analytics
leads.description: Hi HN! Quick story how it started: I was a freelance web developer in the past and also worked for several companies on web applications. For some projects we didn’t have analytics at all and we had to ask ourselves too many times what our users actually use in the product. Finding a good solution was painful, since we couldn’t use a consent banner (a lot of customers from the government) and existing tools were hard to set up so nobody took the time. I started with this idea already many years ago, but only really got to develop it in the past year. So what is Privatrak? A product tracking tool which is simple to set up and doesn’t require any code for most use cases. It can be used just by tagging elements on your site in the browser. From that, funnels and analytics dashboards can be created. I also wanted to make it as easy as possible to use with AI agents, hence there is a MCP server which can be used to question the data and set up the project (every change an AI agent makes is tracked and can also easily be undone). It doesn’t store any sensitive user data and can be used without a consent banner or cookies. Sessions are calculated based on a hash that consists of the users IP address + user agent + random rotating salt (IP address and user agent are never stored) and are aggregated for each day, so the data basically only points at a group of users in the end. In many cases this is fine. Often you are only curious about a specific feature or trends and not what a specific user did. If you need to track people over multiple days or need session replays, this is not the right tool. My main goal in posting here is to get some feedback for the product. Is the daily cutoff for sessions a dealbreaker for you? I just launched it and currently only have a handful of people actually using it. I built a demo project for everybody to see how it looks without having to sign up: https://demo.privatrak.com/

leads.title: Show HN: Clawdline – Manage Claude Code/Codex sessions across computers
leads.description: I built Clawdline to manage Claude Code and Codex sessions across multiple computers in one place. It runs on multiple computers (Mac and Linux), and you can see all of your sessions in one list. Each session reports its status (working, completed, or needs attention). You can also manage all your sessions and receive notifications from your phone (web app). Herdr, T3 Code, and Orca already cover a lot of this space, and there’s overlap. When I started building Clawdline, I didn't know about Herdr, T3 Code, or Orca. So I built it to fit my own dev workflow. At first, I used Swift to build a Mac app, but I realized that it wouldn't work if I also wanted to support Linux. So I decided to rewrite it in Go. Now it can support both of them. Main Features: - Cross Machine Agent Communication: You can ask a root session ("Local") on your Mac to start a new session ("Remote") on a remote Linux machine. Once the remote session finishes its work, it notifies the root ("Local") session. - Cross Agent Communication: You can use one root session to create tasks need multiple agents. They can communicate with each other through clawdline - Scheduled Task with Webhook: You can create scheduled tasks and combine them with your service (use webhooks to trigger new agent sessions) - Board System: tasks control for Feature, Issue, Epic, Refactor, Plan - Snippet/Playbook: If there are commands you use them very often, snippet can help you - TODO: lightweight tasks - Note: Agents can leave notes to you if they need your attention - Agent Squad: assign role to any task or session - Archive: you can archive sessions and see it in one place - Others: Intelligence session naming, Image/Video display, Voice input, Machine monitor, Usage Monitor, Dev Stack Run, Deploy progress monitor... This project is open source and I have used Claude & Codex to do independent reviews on Clawdline, Herdr, T3 and Orca. (you can find the reviews on the website.) The work still needs further input and feedback. Hope this helps other developers improve their devs! :)

leads.title: Ask HN: Are Apple app reviewers sharing app ideas?
leads.description: Not accusing anyone but let me explain. I like telling stories to my kid when he goes to bed. Since there are a lot of evening doing this, I started inventing these stories and to keep it a bit interesting I started asking him about what or how would he change the outcomes, and then it struck me. What if I create stories where readers can interact and change the outcomes. So for the past year I was working on this game engine that would allow to create stories and defined rules, game mechanics per game, and allow players to pick their own route through the story. I finished the app and wrote a couple of stories and registered the app on the App Store. At that point (more then 3 months ago) there was no other app with that name. In that period I sent it up for review, which took a more then week every time, and it was rejected 3 times for the stupid reasons: - in app image text not visible: I used a small cover image from stories, and one of them had this text on a wall in the background - they've said text unreadable - I picked the secondary category for the app as books: I thought that games would be a good fit for the main category, why not pick books for the second - well this was not right again - When I selected the App Store countries I also selected China: they've said that books are only allowed to be published in China if I register as book published there - so I had to remove it from that store, although they said I cannot pick books as my secondary category After all 3 reviews, which each of them took me around 10 minutes to fix and re-request another approval check, took weeks in-between. The last and final one took 1 whole month, and this after requesting an expedited review 3 times, because no body would answer the feedback dev-reviewer board. Anyway, I was so happy when yesterday my app got finally approved and it landed on the store. So as anyone would do, I picked up my phone and searched for it. And yeah, it was there, but there was another app with the same name, same idea, same everything (almost). My happiness immediately faded, and I was so disappointed in me, that I did not see it before, but then I got angry. I immediately checked the "What's new" section of this app, just to find out that it was just published, like 2 weeks ago (suspicious). I then went into this developer's account to see their other apps, and to my astonishment, they are all copied apps, and all of them first released 2 weeks ago. I search all these apps, and yes there's another app with those same names. And then it struck me, could it be that I got delayed for a whole month, while somebody just copied my idea, or other devs ideas while they wait and cannot do anything about it, just to find out they've came second. With AI being so fast, you cannot compete any more with it. You can nowadays recreate apps in just hours, while the original dev might have needed months, or years to reach the same point. Bottom line is, that I do not point fingers, but my experience raised some doubts in my mind. Just wanted to share this with you and to ask if anyone had this in the past?

leads.title: Looking for a tech job is a helpless data-entry nightmare
leads.description: I spent hundred of hours (distributed over many days) filling my resume data to freshly developed forms made specifically to the hiring process of one or two companies, even though I feel like I have a top 10% resume and years of in hands-down software development experience. I love solving problems, it's part of me. I know it has got a lot harder to land a development gig but I've worked with modern stuff like AI-generated briefs for meetings, bug logs automatically sent emails to responsible developers, at a point I had an Agent dedicated to verifying how well our code was written so I feel like I've kept up with the innovations, and skills. But I have no idea how to land a job in software development anymore: nothing seems enough. I have tried for over a year and the only reason I can withstand this much waiting while seeking a job in that field is because of my exceptional employment history (including working to Silicon Valley companies), but it has got to a point I am worried. I've asked my friends who are also developers and they feel similarly, we do not know where to dedicate our effors, as if the competency of software engineers were transformed irrelevant because of AI. We know what happened, we just don't know what to do with all the competency we embody. I've taken a liking to working as a bartender in my local city, because that's kind of the only job I can land lately, but as soon as my degree in Computer Engineering is mentioned I'm set aside as a anti-social computer expert who will never take a low-paying job like "this". (Secretly I found it very fun, fullfilling in a way I never thought I needed because money was my priority at the beggining of the carreer) How the hell do we transform this competency and learning ability of software engineers into desireable company-adding value skills? (I swear this is not generated by AI, I don't even know how to prove anymore)

Develop and maintain a scalable compliance roadmap aligned with business growth and customer requirements. Coordinate security incidents and drive continuous improvements to our security processes and controls. leads.description: Role summary: At Differential Bio, our mission is to unlock the potential of the bioeconomy by fixing how biological R&D and scale-up are done. This role is focused on research , including creating hybrid models that combine mechanistic and machine learning approaches to predict how microbial fermentations behave , and that keep working when we move to a new organism, a new sensor, or a larger reactor. You’ll own your research projects from scoping to delivery, with support from our modelling lead but with autonomy and independence. You’ll work closely with our wet lab, dry lab and software teams, and identify which data you need to generate from our robotic lab. Key responsibilities: Hybrid bioprocess modelling Develop hybrid mechanistic/ML cell response models that predict fermentation outcomes (growth, titer, yield, productivity) from process and sensor data. Fuse time-series signals from process analytical technology (Raman, NIR, dielectric spectroscopy, dissolved oxygen, off-gas) with offline analytics. Build mechanistic backbones (e.g., kinetic/ODE models, genome-scale metabolic models) that constrain learning and generate synthetic training data. Develop machine learning surrogate models for computationally costly mechanistic simulations. Quantify uncertainty so that models can be trusted in high-stakes production settings. Transfer across organisms and scales Design models that carry over from benchtop to pilot and production scale, and across various microbes including bacteria and yeast. Use transfer learning and representation learning to make good predictions for new strains and processes with little data. Develop scale-transferable reactor characterisations and predictive KPI models for scale-up. Real-time Model-Predictive Control Build the AI/ML layer for Nonlinear Model Predictive Control (NMPC) and reinforcement-learning-based feeding strategies to optimize titer, rate, and yield dynamically. Fuse real-time data from Process Analytical Technology (PAT) and soft sensors (e.g., Raman, NIR) into dynamic state estimators to drive closed-loop bioreactor actuators (feed, air, agitation). Prototype simpler, deployable steps along the way, such as deviation detection and operator alerts Design control frameworks to proactively resolve metabolic bottlenecks and robustly account for model uncertainty, batch-to-batch variability, and inherent bioprocess stochasticity. Qualifications: PhD in machine learning, bioengineering, computational biology, or a related field, or a Master’s degree with 3+ years of relevant industry experience. Strong research independence; ability to scope and execute novel scientific work from start to finish. Demonstrated evidence of research contributions, including (but not limited to): peer-reviewed journal or conference papers, conference attendance, open-source contributions. Strong Python and modern ML tooling (e.g., PyTorch/JAX, scikit-learn)

leads.title: Stage: Afdeling Finance
leads.description: Over Nedlin Nedlin is een industriële textielverzorger voor Healthcare, Hospitality en Industry, waar veiligheid, kwaliteit, continu verbeteren en verantwoord ondernemen centraal staan. Als groeiend B-Corp familiebedrijf investeren we graag in jong talent en versterken we de verbinding tussen onderwijs en arbeidsmarkt. Daarom bieden we studenten de kans om praktijkervaring op te doen, zich te ontwikkelen en Nedlin te leren kennen, met waar mogelijk mooie doorgroeikansen na het afstuderen. De stageopdrachten Binnen de afdeling Finance hebben we meerdere uitdagende stageopdrachten openstaan, van AI en automatisering tot data en procesoptimalisatie. Samen kijken we naar jouw interesses en opleiding om te bepalen welke opdracht het beste bij jou past. Maak onze kwartaalafsluiting slimmer : Onderzoek hoe we de kwartaalafsluiting sneller en efficiënter kunnen maken door handmatige werkzaamheden te automatiseren. Jouw uitdaging: Ontwikkel een slimme, betrouwbare en zoveel mogelijk geautomatiseerde werkwijze. Haal meer uit AI binnen Purchase-to-Pay : Onderzoek hoe AI ons Purchase-to-Pay-proces verder kan optimaliseren en automatiseren. Jouw uitdaging: Ontdek welke processtappen we met AI nog slimmer kunnen maken. Bereid Nedlin voor op Peppol : Onderzoek wat de verdere uitrol van Peppol betekent en maak een praktisch implementatieplan. Jouw uitdaging: Zorg voor een toekomstbestendige integratie van Peppol in ons financiële proces. Ontwerp het debiteurenproces van de toekomst : Onderzoek hoe technologie en automatisering ons aanmaningsproces slimmer en efficiënter kunnen maken. Jouw uitdaging: Ontwerp een slim en datagedreven debiteurenproces. Van data naar inzicht : Onderzoek hoe we onze data, databronnen en dashboards slimmer kunnen inrichten. Jouw uitdaging: Zorg dat betrouwbare data sneller en eenvoudiger beschikbaar is. Maak financiële mailboxen slimmer met AI : Onderzoek hoe we binnenkomende e-mails en documenten met AI en programmeren automatisch kunnen herkennen en verwerken. Jouw uitdaging: Ontwikkel een concept of prototype voor slim mailboxbeheer. Ontdek automatiseringskansen in onze processen : Breng processen binnen Nedlin in kaart en ontdek kansen voor digitalisering, standaardisering en automatisering. Jouw uitdaging: Vertaal jouw inzichten naar concrete verbeteringen voor slimmere en efficiëntere processen. Wat bieden wij? Stagevergoeding: € 400,- bruto per maand voor hbo-studenten (op basis van 40 uur per week); Een leerzame stage binnen één van de modernste en duurzaamste wasserijen van Europa; Ruimte en begeleiding om te werken aan jouw (afstudeer)opdracht; Persoonlijke begeleiding en korte lijnen; Een familiaire en positieve sfeer: samen feestdagen vieren, een jaarlijkse familiedag en leuke uitjes; Kans op een (bij)baan bij Nedlin na afronding van je stage, bij wederzijdse match. Wie ben jij? Je volgt een hbo-opleiding, bijvoorbeeld Commerciële Economie, Business Studies, Facility Management, Accountancy, Finance & Control of International Business. Je werkt zelfstandig, nauwkeurig en proactief. Je communiceert gemakkelijk met verschillende collega’s. Je bent 32 tot 40 uur per week beschikbaar voor een meewerk- en/of afstudeerstage. Je kunt zelfstandig naar onze locatie in Elsloo komen. Je stelt kritische ‘waarom’-vragen en denkt graag in structuren. Je combineert een analytische blik met creatieve oplossingen. Pak het moment Wil jij tijdens je stage niet alleen werken aan een interessante opdracht, maar vooral ook leren, ervaring opdoen en jezelf ontwikkelen? Bij Nedlin krijg je de ruimte om jouw kennis vanuit je opleiding toe te passen in de praktijk, mee te kijken binnen onze organisatie en samen te werken met ervaren collega’s. Maak van jouw stage een waardevolle stap richting je toekomst. Solliciteer eenvoudig via de solliciteerknop. Heb je eerst nog vragen over de stage of de opdracht? With $200+ million in annual revenue and team members based around the globe , Toptal is the world’s largest fully remote workforce . We take the best elements of virtual teams and combine them with a support structure that encourages innovation, social interaction, and fun. We see no borders, move at a fast pace, and are never afraid to break the mold. Position Description We are seeking a highly versatile and experienced Sales Recruiter to join our dynamic team. In this role, you’ll partner closely with our Sales leaders to strategically attract and hire top-tier sales talent across all levels - from individual contributors to VP level. As a key member of our Recruiting team, you’ll act as a true business partner - collaborating with leadership to define search strategies and serving as a trusted advisor to help interview teams hire effectively and efficiently. We are looking for someone who is passionate about delivering world-class candidate experiences, has a strong track record of hiring top sales professionals, and thrives in a collaborative environment. You will own full life-cycle recruiting efforts, influence strategy, and help shape how we attract and engage high-performing candidates. This is a remote position. However, candidates must be located in the United States or Canada. We do not offer visa sponsorship or assistance. Resumes and communication must be submitted in English. Responsibilities: The following information is intended to describe the general nature and level of work being performed. It is not intended to be an exhaustive list of all duties, responsibilities, or required skills. Build and maintain a strong pipeline of highly qualified candidates for all Sales roles, partnering closely with Executive and Sales Leadership teams to ensure hiring goals are met. Proactively source, identify and engage top-performing talent across global markets. Conduct thorough candidate outreach and screening across multiple channels, effectively communicating role details while continuously assessing candidate fit. Design and coordinate customized interview processes that align with Toptal’s high hiring bar and role specific requirements. Act as the primary point of contact for candidates, guiding them through each stage of the interview process and ensuring an exceptional candidate experience. Communicate effectively and consistently with internal teams via Slack and Zoom. leads.title: Show HN: What a major earthquake does to Vancouver
leads.description: About 10 years ago, I attended a presentation by someone who had compiled existing engineering reports to describe the impact of a major earthquake on infrastructure in British Columbia. It was really striking, and it has stayed in the back of my mind ever since. I am now the point of contact for downtown Vancouver in the French community's emergency network, and it drives me nuts that most people I talk to have no emergency kit at home and basically no water. People are shocked, or in denial, when I mention that it could take weeks to restore electricity and that they will have to rely on their own food and water for at least several days. So I decided to build a public-facing site that compiles existing information, as a way to lay out the facts and help convince people, instead of hearing back that "the army will come" or that "there are emergency food reserves" (there aren't). I see this as a citizen initiative, with one main message: go buy some water and canned food, it's your civic duty. I relied on AI agents to compile the information, which is spread across hundreds of reports. With different levels of validation, plus my own review, I am confident the information is reliable, even if some details may not be fully up to date. The process took 2–3 weeks, alongside work, a toddler and a baby! I'm posting it here because: 1) I'm curious to get feedback and suggestions. 2) Many HN readers are on the West Coast or in other seismic areas, so even if you're not in Vancouver, the general recommendations may be of interest. Be smart: buy some food and water. Cheers Thomas

leads.description: If you're looking for a job, do -not- have Claude bulk email every company on "Who's Hiring". These things all look the same and your message is just going to get marked spam. For example, it's painfully obvious that our staff eng role's "combination of distributed execution, workload optimization, and cost-aware infrastructure" is not, in fact, "unusually close" to whatever line on your resume Claude decided is tangentially relevant. Just write a normal email by hand and send it. If you it looks like you spent 5 minutes looking up what we do and are actually excited I'll at least look at your resume; if you spent 0 minutes thinking about the job posting I'm going to spend 0 minutes on this too.

leads.title: Show HN: git-dupe – Version private files alongside a public Git repo
leads.description: Hi HN! I made git-dupe to solve the problem where I have notes, skills, and agent instructions that are part of my personal workflow, so I do not want them committed to the public repo, but at the same time, I want them to be in the project at the correct locations (e.g., AGENTS.md file locations matter), and these files cannot be simply gitignored because I want versioning for them. The solution that I've come upon is versioning those agent files in another repo, say <private-repo> (this repo is private to me and holds the history for my agent files). The project itself is open to the public in another <public-repo>. I overlap the two repos to solve the problem (i.e., they share the same worktree). $ git status --short # the public repo ?? AGENTS.md ?? notes/ $ git dupe init # the private repo Initialized empty Git repository in /home/brian/code/project/.git/dupe/ $ git dupe add notes/ AGENTS.md # the private repo hint: notes is now hidden from the project's Git; run from the root, 'git dupe unhide -- notes' stops hiding it $ git dupe commit -m "Notes and agent instructions" # the private repo [main (root-commit) 3eb3af9] Notes and agent instructions 3 files changed, 3 insertions(+) create mode 100644 .gitdupe create mode 100644 AGENTS.md create mode 100644 notes/todo.md $ git status --short # the public repo: nothing $ git dupe log --oneline # the private repo: your files 3eb3af9 Notes and agent instructions In short, git-dupe allows two Git repos to share the same worktree, while using native Git for most operations. Most git-dupe commands behave just like normal Git commands, operating on the private repo instead. git-dupe currently supports Linux and macOS, and is under the MIT License; the git-dupe repo contains much more extensive technical documentation documentation for those who are interested. If you have any feedback/questions about git-dupe, feel free to message. I hope it helps! Fun fact: the git-dupe project itself is using git-dupe for versioning.

leads.title: Show HN: Extending X402 for MoR fiat payments and budget attenuation
leads.description: X402 and similar protocols requires crypto native settlement. For freelancers and SMEs under many European tax regimes, it can be a tax nightmare. In this proposal the payment is in FIAT (via a Merchant of Record), and the agents orchestrator can attenuate the budget into smaller, independently revocable sub-budgets for its worker using Biscuits. This is a reference implementation with some described known limitations, not a production system. I'd love to get feedback. Thanks for taking a look!

leads.title: Tell HN: Scribd Breached
leads.description: Not seeing anything posted about this anywhere, received on Monday, 26th of Oct 2026: Subject: Notice of Security Incident This notice is being sent on behalf of Scribd, Inc., the parent company of Scribd, Slideshare, Everand, and Fable, by Epiq, Scribd Inc.’s notification partner. Hello, We are writing to let you know that Scribd, Inc. recently experienced a security incident that may have affected your data. We detected that an unauthorized third party may have gained access to certain user data in one of our systems. After investigating this activity, we found that the third party may have accessed your email address and the following of your information: last 4 digits of your credit card and country, credit card issuer, credit card expiry date, payment history (not including credit card details). We have no evidence that this data has been misused, but we are notifying you out of an abundance of caution so that you can take steps to protect your information.
